games.title: Medical Bacteriology and Entomology Exam 2020/2021: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 2 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following organisms is a Gram-negative diplococcus that ferments maltose and glucose, and is a major cause of bacterial meningitis in older children and young adults?
questions.explanation: Neisseria meningitidis is a Gram-negative diplococcus that ferments both glucose and maltose, differentiating it from Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

questions.q: A patient presents with watery diarrhea after eating improperly cooked seafood. Gram-negative, curved, oxidase-positive rods are isolated from the stool. Which organism is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: Vibrio cholerae is a comma-shaped, oxidase-positive, Gram-negative bacterium associated with waterborne or seafood-associated outbreaks of watery diarrhea.

questions.q: Which of the following vectors is primarily responsible for the transmission of epidemic typhus caused by Rickettsia prowazekii?
questions.explanation: Pediculus humanus humanus (the human body louse) is the vector responsible for transmitting Rickettsia prowazekii, the agent of epidemic typhus.

questions.q: A patient with a history of a tick bite presents with a characteristic bull's-eye rash (erythema migrans) and flu-like symptoms. The causative agent is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Borrelia burgdorferi, the causative agent of Lyme disease, is a tick-borne spirochete visualized using dark-field microscopy or special stains like Giemsa.

questions.q: Which virulence factor of Streptococcus pyogenes is primarily responsible for preventing phagocytosis and plays a major role in post-streptococcal sequelae?
questions.explanation: The M protein of Streptococcus pyogenes inhibits phagocytosis and is antigenically related to human myocardial antigens, leading to rheumatic fever.

questions.q: Which laboratory test is most appropriate for the definitive laboratory diagnosis of active pulmonary tuberculosis in a patient with a productive cough?
options: Serum IgG ELISA against Mycobacterium tuberculosis
questions.explanation: Acid-fast staining (Ziehl-Neelsen) and culture on Lowenstein-Jensen medium provide definitive evidence of active M. tuberculosis infection.

questions.q: A 25-year-old sexually active female presents with dysuria and a mucocervical discharge. Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) confirms an obligate intracellular bacterium that lacks a classic peptidoglycan cell wall. What is the organism?
questions.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular pathogen with a unique biphasic developmental cycle that lacks a rigid peptidoglycan layer.

questions.q: Which arthropod vector transmits the parasite responsible for endemic malaria?
questions.explanation: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium species, which are transmitted exclusively through the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

questions.q: A patient presents with severe muscle spasms, lockjaw, and risus sardonicus following a deep puncture wound from a rusty nail. The toxin produced by this organism acts by inhibiting the release of which neurotransmitters?
questions.explanation: Tetanospasmin, produced by Clostridium tetani, is a retrograde axonal toxin that blocks the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine in the spinal cord.

questions.q: Which of the following bacteria is a leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia and is characterized by being a Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococcus that is optochin-sensitive?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococcus that is alpha-hemolytic and susceptible to optochin.

games.title: Gastritis and Peptic Ulcer Disease: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of primary chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease in children?
questions.explanation: Helicobacter pylori infection is the primary cause of chronic active gastritis and primary peptic ulcer disease in pediatric populations.

questions.q: How does peptic ulcer disease typically present in infants and toddlers under 2 years of age?
options: Feeding intolerance, vomiting, and upper GI bleeding
questions.explanation: Infants and young toddlers typically present with non-specific symptoms such as feeding intolerance, vomiting, hematemesis, or melena rather than localized epigastric pain.

questions.q: Which non-invasive diagnostic test is most appropriate for confirming Helicobacter pylori eradication 4 to 8 weeks after completing treatment in a 7-year-old child?
options: Serum H. pylori IgG antibody test
questions.explanation: The monoclonal stool antigen test or urea breath test is recommended for confirming eradication because serum IgG antibodies can remain positive for months to years post-treatment.

questions.q: What is the gold standard diagnostic procedure for peptic ulcer disease and for obtaining mucosal tissue for Helicobacter pylori testing in children?
questions.explanation: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy with mucosal biopsy for histopathology and rapid urease testing or culture is the gold standard for diagnosing PUD and H. pylori in children.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child with a Helicobacter pylori-positive duodenal ulcer is started on treatment in an area with low clarithromycin resistance. Which regimen is recommended as first-line eradication therapy?
questions.explanation: Standard first-line triple therapy for H. pylori consists of a proton pump inhibitor combined with amoxicillin and clarithromycin (or metronidazole) for 14 days.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with severe thermal burns over 40% of his body develops hematemesis. What specific stress-related ulcer is he at risk for?
questions.explanation: Stress ulcers occurring specifically in severely burned patients are known as Curling ulcers, resulting from mucosal ischemia due to hypovolemia.

questions.q: A 4-year-old girl with a severe traumatic brain injury develops acute gastric mucosal ulceration and upper GI hemorrhage. What is the primary mechanism underlying this condition (Cushing ulcer)?
options: Vagal overstimulation causing hypersecretion of gastric acid
Direct thermal injury to the gastric epithelium
questions.explanation: Cushing ulcers are caused by raised intracranial pressure leading to excessive vagal stimulation and acid hypersecretion.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with sudden-onset severe, diffuse abdominal pain, guarding, and rebound tenderness. An upright chest X-ray reveals free air under the diaphragm. What is the most urgent next step in management?
questions.explanation: Pneumoperitoneum indicates a perforated viscus, which requires urgent surgical consultation and emergency operative repair.

questions.q: An 8-year-old boy presents with lower extremity purpura, colicky abdominal pain, arthralgia, and microscopic hematuria. What endoscopic finding is characteristic of gastrointestinal involvement in this disease?
questions.explanation: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) causes leukocytoclastic vasculitis of the GI tract, presenting with submucosal purpura, mucosal edema, and focal ulcerations.

questions.q: A 14-year-old girl with juvenile idiopathic arthritis requires long-term NSAID therapy. Which mechanism best explains how NSAIDs increase her risk of gastric mucosal injury?
options: Inhibition of COX-1 leading to reduced mucosal prostaglandin synthesis
Direct stimulation of gastrin release by G cells
questions.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), decreasing prostaglandin synthesis and thereby impairing mucosal blood flow, bicarbonate secretion, and mucus production.

games.title: Disorders of the Vagina and Breast: case showdown
games.topic: Disorders of the Vagina and Breast
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with a painless, highly mobile, well-circumscribed mass in her right breast that she noticed two months ago. Ultrasound reveals a 2 cm well-defined, hypoechoic solid lesion with smooth margins and no microcalcifications. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast lesion in young women, presenting as a firm, mobile, well-circumscribed mass.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with spontaneous, single-duct bloody discharge from her left nipple. Physical examination reveals no palpable breast masses, axillary lymphadenopathy, or skin changes, and mammography is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Intraductal papilloma is the most common cause of spontaneous, unilateral bloody nipple discharge in premenopausal women without a palpable mass.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with a firm, painless mass in her left breast three weeks after a seatbelt injury in a minor motor vehicle collision. Mammography reveals an irregular mass with coarse calcifications, and core biopsy shows lipid-laden macrophages and multinucleated giant cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fat necrosis of the breast typically follows local trauma, presenting as a painless mass with histological findings of foamy lipid-laden macrophages and giant cells.

questions.q: A 58-year-old woman presents with persistent scaly, erythematous, eczematous changes of the left nipple and areola that failed to respond to topical corticosteroids. A punch biopsy of the affected nipple skin shows large malignant cells with abundant clear cytoplasm infiltrating the epidermis. What is the underlying condition most commonly associated with this finding?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
questions.explanation: Paget disease of the nipple manifests as eczematous nipple skin changes and is almost universally associated with an underlying ductal carcinoma (DCIS or invasive ductal carcinoma).

questions.q: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the clinic due to vaginal bleeding and a soft, cluster-of-grapes mass protruding from her vagina. Biopsy demonstrates primitive round and spindle-shaped cells with a prominent subepithelial cambium layer. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides) classically presents in young girls under 5 years old as a grape-like mass protruding from the vagina.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman presents with irregular vaginal spotting. Her biological mother took a synthetic medication during pregnancy in the 1970s to prevent threatened abortion. Which vaginal neoplasm is this patient at greatest risk for developing?
questions.explanation: In utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES) strongly predisposes female offspring to vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with rapid right breast enlargement accompanied by erythema, edema, and a dimpled 'peau d'orange' appearance of the overlying skin. She is afebrile and a 10-day course of empiric antibiotics produced no improvement. Which pathological mechanism is directly responsible for her skin appearance?
options: Tumor emboli invading dermal lymphatic channels
Rupture of an infected epithelial breast cyst
Extensive granulomatous inflammation of subcutaneous fat
questions.explanation: Inflammatory breast cancer presents with characteristic peau d'orange due to tumor emboli obstructing dermal lymphatic channels.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with a rapidly enlarging, painless 7 cm mass in her left breast. Core needle biopsy demonstrates marked stromal hypercellularity forming leaf-like projections lined by benign epithelium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Phyllodes tumors are fibroepithelial neoplasms characterized by hypercellular stroma and leaf-like architectural projections, commonly presenting as large, rapidly growing masses in older premenopausal women.

games.title: Acute Viral Hepatitis: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 24-year-old male presents with a 5-day history of low-grade fever, anorexia, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and dark urine after returning from a trip to Southeast Asia. Physical examination reveals scleral icterus and tender hepatomegaly, while lab work shows serum ALT of 2,400 U/L and AST of 1,800 U/L. Which serological test is most specific for establishing the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: IgM anti-HAV is the diagnostic marker of choice for acute Hepatitis A virus infection, which commonly presents after travel to endemic areas via fecal-oral transmission.

questions.q: A 30-year-old female presents with fatigue, malaise, and jaundice for one week. Serum lab testing shows ALT 1,550 U/L, AST 1,200 U/L, positive HBsAg, positive IgM anti-HBc, and negative anti-HBs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of HBsAg combined with IgM anti-HBc confirms a diagnosis of acute Hepatitis B infection.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male with a history of intravenous drug use presents with acute onset of nausea, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and severe jaundice. Laboratory testing demonstrates an elevated serum ALT of 1,850 U/L and a positive anti-HCV antibody result. What is the next best step to confirm active acute Hepatitis C infection?
questions.explanation: Serum HCV RNA PCR testing is required to confirm active infection, as anti-HCV antibodies only indicate exposure and cannot distinguish between acute, chronic, or resolved infection.

questions.q: A 26-year-old pregnant female at 28 weeks gestation presents with acute jaundice, fever, and severe vomiting after returning from a region with contaminated water supplies. Laboratory tests show serum ALT 3,100 U/L and acute serologies for HAV, HBV, and HCV are all negative. Which viral pathogen is the most likely cause of her acute hepatitis?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis E virus causes waterborne epidemics of acute hepatitis and carries a high risk of fulminant hepatic failure and mortality in pregnant women.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male with known chronic Hepatitis B (HBsAg positive) presents with sudden clinical deterioration, worsening jaundice, and an acute ALT spike to 1,400 U/L. Serological testing for acute HAV and acute HCV is negative. Which pathogen should be suspected as the cause of this acute flare?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis D virus requires the presence of HBsAg to replicate and can cause severe acute flares when superinfecting patients with chronic Hepatitis B.

questions.q: A 32-year-old male is diagnosed with acute, uncomplicated Hepatitis B virus infection after presenting with mild jaundice and a serum ALT of 1,200 U/L. He is fully oriented, hemodynamically stable, and has a normal prothrombin time/INR. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
options: Supportive care and outpatient clinical monitoring
questions.explanation: Over 95% of immunocompetent adults clear acute Hepatitis B spontaneously, making supportive care and monitoring the recommended primary management for uncomplicated cases.

questions.q: A 23-year-old unvaccinated nursing student suffers a deep needle-stick injury while caring for a patient known to be HBsAg-positive. Serological testing of the student confirms she is negative for both HBsAg and anti-HBs. What is the most appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis for this student?
options: Single dose of Hepatitis B vaccine only
HBIG combined with initiation of the Hepatitis B vaccine series
questions.explanation: Unvaccinated individuals exposed to HBsAg-positive blood should receive both Hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) and the first dose of the Hepatitis B vaccine series as soon as possible.

questions.q: A 38-year-old female with acute Hepatitis A presents to the emergency department with progressive lethargy, confusion, and asterixis on examination. Laboratory studies reveal an INR of 2.8 and total bilirubin of 18 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: The onset of hepatic encephalopathy and coagulopathy (INR > 1.5) in acute hepatitis defines acute liver failure, warranting immediate referral for urgent liver transplantation evaluation.

games.title: Antifungals, Antivirals, Antihelminthics & Antiprotozoals: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of caspofungin?
options: Inhibition of beta-1,3-D-glucan synthesis in the fungal cell wall
Binding to ergosterol to form membrane pores
questions.explanation: Caspofungin belongs to the echinocandin class and works by inhibiting the synthesis of beta-1,3-D-glucan, an essential component of the fungal cell wall.

questions.q: A patient receiving intravenous amphotericin B for invasive candidiasis develops acute renal impairment. Which pattern of electrolyte abnormalities is most characteristic of amphotericin B toxicity?
questions.explanation: Amphotericin B causes nephrotoxicity leading to renal tubular acidosis and wasting of potassium and magnesium, resulting in hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of oseltamivir in the treatment of influenza infections?
options: Inhibition of the viral M2 proton channel
Competitive inhibition of viral DNA polymerase
Inhibition of viral neuraminidase to prevent viral release
questions.explanation: Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor that prevents the cleavage of sialic acid residues, thereby blocking the release of newly formed influenza virions from infected host cells.

questions.q: A patient receiving antiviral therapy with ganciclovir for cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis must be monitored closely for which major dose-limiting toxicity?
questions.explanation: The primary dose-limiting side effect of ganciclovir is bone marrow suppression, particularly neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of mebendazole against intestinal nematodes?
options: Hyperpolarization of parasite muscle cells via GABA receptor activation
Inhibition of microtubule synthesis by binding to beta-tubulin
Paralysis of worms by inducing intracellular calcium influx
Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
questions.explanation: Benzimidazoles such as mebendazole work by selectively binding to helminthic beta-tubulin, inhibiting microtubule polymerization and glucose uptake.

questions.q: Which antiparasitic agent acts by increasing cell membrane permeability to calcium, causing severe spasms and paralysis of target worms, and is the drug of choice for Schistosoma infections?
questions.explanation: Praziquantel increases the permeability of parasite cell membranes to calcium, leading to massive contraction and paralysis of schistosomes and trematodes.

questions.q: A patient taking metronidazole consumes alcohol and experiences severe flushing, nausea, vomiting, and tachycardia. What is the mechanism underlying this adverse reaction?
options: Synergistic activation of central GABA receptors
Direct mucosal irritation of the upper gastrointestinal tract
questions.explanation: Metronidazole inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing an accumulation of acetaldehyde when co-consumed with alcohol, which leads to a disulfiram-like reaction.

questions.q: Which antimalarial agent specifically targets the dormant liver hypnozoite stage of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale to prevent disease relapse?
questions.explanation: Primaquine is an 8-aminoquinoline that eliminates dormant liver-stage hypnozoites of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale, preventing disease relapse.

games.title: Acute and chronic diarrhoea: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of loperamide in the management of acute non-specific diarrhoea?
options: Peripheral mu-opioid receptor agonist causing decreased intestinal motility
5-HT3 receptor antagonist reducing mucosal fluid secretion
Enkephalinase inhibitor enhancing endogenous enkephalin action
Bile acid sequestrant binding luminal osmotic toxins
questions.explanation: Loperamide acts as a selective peripheral mu-opioid receptor agonist in the myenteric plexus, slowing intestinal transit and increasing absorption time.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient who underwent terminal ileal resection 2 years ago presents with chronic watery diarrhoea. Which medication is the most appropriate targeted treatment for this patient's diarrhoea?
questions.explanation: Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant indicated for chronic diarrhoea caused by bile acid malabsorption following terminal ileal disease or resection.

questions.q: A 28-year-old traveller takes bismuth subsalicylate for acute traveller's diarrhoea. Which characteristic, benign side effect should the patient be warned about to prevent unnecessary anxiety?
options: Black discoloration of the stool and tongue
questions.explanation: Bismuth reacts with microenvironmental sulfur in the gastrointestinal tract to form bismuth sulfide, which harmlessly darkens the stool and tongue.

questions.q: A 58-year-old patient with severe flushing and chronic watery diarrhoea is diagnosed with a carcinoid tumour. Which drug is specifically indicated to suppress this hormone-mediated secretory diarrhoea?
questions.explanation: Octreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analogue that suppresses the secretion of gastrointestinal hormones, effective in controlling carcinoid-induced secretory diarrhoea.

questions.q: Racecadotril is used as an adjunctive oral treatment for acute diarrhoea. What is its primary mechanism of action?
questions.explanation: Racecadotril inhibits peripheral enkephalinase, preventing the degradation of endogenous enkephalins to reduce hypersecretion of fluid and electrolytes into the lumen.

questions.q: A 72-year-old hospitalized patient develops severe Clostridioides difficile infection. Which targeted macrocyclic antibiotic selectively inhibits C. difficile RNA polymerase while preserving normal gut microflora?
questions.explanation: Fidaxomicin is a narrow-spectrum macrocyclic antibiotic that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase, specifically targeting Clostridioides difficile with minimal impact on normal commensal flora.

questions.q: Co-phenotrope (Lomotil) contains diphenoxylate combined with a subtherapeutic dose of atropine. What is the primary purpose of including atropine in this formulation?
options: To synergistically block histamine H2 receptors in the gut
To deter intentional abuse and overdose by inducing unpleasant anticholinergic effects at high doses
To directly increase colonic sodium and fluid absorption
questions.explanation: Subtherapeutic atropine is added to diphenoxylate formulations to discourage deliberate drug abuse by causing distressing anticholinergic side effects if consumed in excessive quantities.

questions.q: In patients with refractory carcinoid syndrome diarrhoea despite optimal somatostatin analogue therapy, telotristat ethyl may be added. What is the mechanism of action of telotristat ethyl?
options: Inhibits tryptophan hydroxylase, reducing peripheral serotonin synthesis
Directly stimulates sodium absorption via SGLT-1 in the colon
questions.explanation: Telotristat ethyl orally inhibits tryptophan hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme in serotonin biosynthesis, thereby decreasing serotonin production and controlling carcinoid diarrhoea.
